items.title: Build a Local Voice Assistant on Jetson Orin Nano with Gemma4
items.summary: Author: 子賢, CAVEDU. Tested with JetPack 6.2. The original article takes inspiration from NVIDIA's GTC Taipei 2026 demonstration of a voice assistant on Jetson Orin Nano. Speech recognition, text-to-speech, visual analysis, and model inference can run locally after the software and models have been downloaded. This walkthrough combines Gemma4 E2B for language and image reasoning, NVIDIA parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 for speech recognition, and Kokoro for speech output. The ASR model described by the source supports English and multiple European languages; do not assume Chinese transcription support from this configuration. Hardware Use a Jetson Orin Nano Super developer kit, preferably with an SSD, plus a keyboard, mouse, display, camera, microphone, and speaker. The webcam microphone and display speakers can be used where supported. 1. Install system packages sudo apt update sudo apt install -y git build-essential cmake curl wget pkg-config python3-pip python3-venv python3-dev alsa-utils pulseaudio-utils v4l-utils psmisc ffmpeg libsndfile1 2. Prepare memory The application uses much of the available RAM. The source creates an 8 GB swap file. Check for an existing swap file and fstab entry before repeating these commands: sudo fallocate -l 8G /swapfile sudo chmod 600 /swapfile sudo mkswap /swapfile sudo swapon /swapfile echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab To reclaim memory, the source temporarily stops the following services and applications. Only stop them if they are not needed for another workload: sudo systemctl stop docker 2 > /dev/null || true sudo systemctl stop containerd 2 > /dev/null || true pkill -f tracker-miner-fs-3 || true pkill -f gnome-software || true free -h 3. Build llama.cpp with CUDA The source estimates 40–60 minutes for compilation. The clone URL below corrects the original article's .gi suffix typo to .git. cd ~ git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp.git cd llama.cpp cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES= "87" -DGGML_NATIVE=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --build build --config Release -j4 4. Download the language model and vision projector The language-model GGUF handles language inference; the multimodal projector processes visual inputs for the model. mkdir -p ~/models && cd ~/models wget -O gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-E2B-it-GGUF/resolve/90f9618340396838ee7ff5b0ba2da27da62953d3/gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf wget -O mmproj-gemma4-e2b-f16.gguf https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/gemma-4-E2B-it-GGUF/resolve/4b90c7b785141802608550fc3cd3c715201532e2/mmproj-gemma-4-e2b-it-f16.gguf ls -lh 5. Start the model server Keep this terminal running; the Python assistant will send requests to it from another terminal. ~/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server -m ~/models/gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf --mmproj ~/models/mmproj-gemma4-e2b-f16.gguf -c 2048 --image-min-tokens 70 --image-max-tokens 70 --ubatch-size 512 --batch-size 512 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 -ngl 99 --flash-attn on --no-mmproj-offload --jinja -np 1 This reproduces the source's network binding. Keep the unauthenticated development server on a trusted network, or bind to localhost when only the local assistant needs it. CLI compatibility can change with llama.cpp revisions. 6. Install the assistant example Open another terminal: cd ~ git clone https://github.com/asierarranz/Cool_Demos.git cd ~/Cool_Demos/Gemma4 python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install --upgrade pip pip install opencv-python-headless onnx_asr kokoro-onnx soundfile huggingface-hub numpy 7. Select audio and camera devices List recording devices: arecord -l export MIC_DEVICE = "plughw:0,0" Replace 0,0 with your microphone's card and device numbers. List playback sinks and select the speaker: pactl list short sinks export SPK_DEVICE = "alsa_output.platform-3510000.hda.hdmi-stereo" The sink above is the source's HDMI example. Use the name actually returned on your system. The executable command uses SPK_DEVICE . List cameras and select the appropriate video index: v4l2-ctl --list-devices export WEBCAM = 0 export VOICE = "af_jessica" Other Kokoro voices named in the source include af_nova, am_puck, bf_emma, and am_onyx. Check the installed voice configuration. Record three seconds and play it back: arecord -D "$MIC_DEVICE" -f S16_LE -r 16000 -c 1 -d 3 /tmp/test.wav paplay --device= "$SPK_DEVICE" /tmp/test.wav 8. Run the assistant cd ~/Cool_Demos/Gemma4 python3 Gemma4_vla.py The first run downloads the speech-recognition and speech-synthesis models and may take several minutes. Once loaded, press Space to record, speak, then press Space again to stop. The program transcribes the recording, sends the text to llama-server, and speaks the model's response. When the assistant determines that visual information is needed, it can capture a camera image and use it in the response. The source asks, “Do you see anyone in front of you?” , triggering the Gemma decided to LOOK! path and a classroom-scene description. Reference: Cool_Demos by asierarranz , Gemma4 E2B , and Parakeet model . English adaptation of CAVEDU's original tutorial . Original author: 子賢. Commands reflect the source setup, with the clone-URL typo corrected and the speaker variable clarified. Screenshots retain their original labels. This translation does not constitute a new hardware test.

Author: 子賢, CAVEDU. Tested with JetPack 6.2.

The original article takes inspiration from NVIDIA's GTC Taipei 2026 demonstration of a voice assistant on Jetson Orin Nano. Speech recognition, text-to-speech, visual analysis, and model inference can run locally after the software and models have been downloaded.

This walkthrough combines Gemma4 E2B for language and image reasoning, NVIDIA parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 for speech recognition, and Kokoro for speech output. The ASR model described by the source supports English and multiple European languages; do not assume Chinese transcription support from this configuration.

Hardware

Use a Jetson Orin Nano Super developer kit, preferably with an SSD, plus a keyboard, mouse, display, camera, microphone, and speaker. The webcam microphone and display speakers can be used where supported.

1. Install system packages 
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git build-essential cmake curl wget pkg-config python3-pip python3-venv python3-dev alsa-utils pulseaudio-utils v4l-utils psmisc ffmpeg libsndfile1
2. Prepare memory

The application uses much of the available RAM. The source creates an 8 GB swap file. Check for an existing swap file and fstab entry before repeating these commands:

sudo fallocate -l 8G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

To reclaim memory, the source temporarily stops the following services and applications. Only stop them if they are not needed for another workload:

sudo systemctl stop docker 2>/dev/null || true
sudo systemctl stop containerd 2>/dev/null || true
pkill -f tracker-miner-fs-3 || true
pkill -f gnome-software || true
free -h

3. Build llama.cpp with CUDA

The source estimates 40–60 minutes for compilation. The clone URL below corrects the original article's .gi suffix typo to .git.

cd ~
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp.git
cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="87" -DGGML_NATIVE=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --config Release -j4


4. Download the language model and vision projector

The language-model GGUF handles language inference; the multimodal projector processes visual inputs for the model.

mkdir -p ~/models && cd ~/models
wget -O gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-E2B-it-GGUF/resolve/90f9618340396838ee7ff5b0ba2da27da62953d3/gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf
wget -O mmproj-gemma4-e2b-f16.gguf https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/gemma-4-E2B-it-GGUF/resolve/4b90c7b785141802608550fc3cd3c715201532e2/mmproj-gemma-4-e2b-it-f16.gguf
ls -lh


5. Start the model server

Keep this terminal running; the Python assistant will send requests to it from another terminal.

~/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server -m ~/models/gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf --mmproj ~/models/mmproj-gemma4-e2b-f16.gguf -c 2048 --image-min-tokens 70 --image-max-tokens 70 --ubatch-size 512 --batch-size 512 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 -ngl 99 --flash-attn on --no-mmproj-offload --jinja -np 1

This reproduces the source's network binding. Keep the unauthenticated development server on a trusted network, or bind to localhost when only the local assistant needs it. CLI compatibility can change with llama.cpp revisions.


6. Install the assistant example

Open another terminal:

cd ~
git clone https://github.com/asierarranz/Cool_Demos.git
cd ~/Cool_Demos/Gemma4
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install opencv-python-headless onnx_asr kokoro-onnx soundfile huggingface-hub numpy


7. Select audio and camera devices

List recording devices:

arecord -l
export MIC_DEVICE="plughw:0,0"

Replace 0,0 with your microphone's card and device numbers.

List playback sinks and select the speaker:

pactl list short sinks
export SPK_DEVICE="alsa_output.platform-3510000.hda.hdmi-stereo"

The sink above is the source's HDMI example. Use the name actually returned on your system. The executable command uses SPK_DEVICE.

List cameras and select the appropriate video index:

v4l2-ctl --list-devices
export WEBCAM=0
export VOICE="af_jessica"

Other Kokoro voices named in the source include af_nova, am_puck, bf_emma, and am_onyx. Check the installed voice configuration.

Record three seconds and play it back:

arecord -D "$MIC_DEVICE" -f S16_LE -r 16000 -c 1 -d 3 /tmp/test.wav
paplay --device="$SPK_DEVICE" /tmp/test.wav

8. Run the assistant 
cd ~/Cool_Demos/Gemma4
python3 Gemma4_vla.py

The first run downloads the speech-recognition and speech-synthesis models and may take several minutes. Once loaded, press Space to record, speak, then press Space again to stop. The program transcribes the recording, sends the text to llama-server, and speaks the model's response.



When the assistant determines that visual information is needed, it can capture a camera image and use it in the response. The source asks, “Do you see anyone in front of you?”, triggering the Gemma decided to LOOK! path and a classroom-scene description.

Reference: Cool_Demos by asierarranz, Gemma4 E2B, and Parakeet model.

items.title: AAMP Video Buy vs VAST Tag: The Stitcher Only Reads XML the Agent Never Fetched
items.summary: On 13 November 2025, IAB Tech Lab released Agentic Real Time Framework (ARTF) v1.0 for public comment . The press release frames containerized agents sitting beside OpenRTB inside the same data center, not replacing the auction object underneath. Trade coverage situates that work inside the wider AAMP umbrella: negotiate and enrich upstairs, still transact on familiar rails. If you run SSAI, a CTV ad server, or a DSP seat, the rail that actually schedules the break is still VAST. The buyer agent can return success long before anyone proves that XML exists. What the AAMP side calls a finished video buy Agentic Advertising Management Protocols (AAMP) stack agent interfaces on top of OpenDirect, the Deals API, AdCOM, OpenRTB, and VAST. On the buyer path, a programmatic video line often ends with three artifacts that look like delivery: A task status and a row in Agentic Deals or your Deals Library. A Deals API push (Deal Sync) with adtypes including video, floors, flight dates, and sometimes activation copy aimed at legacy DSP UIs. A VAST endpoint URL or activation_instructions text that tells a human to paste a deal id into a platform console. None of those is the creative envelope. The IAB Deals API spec is explicit that the receiver must still validate every bid request that carries the deal id and must apply targeting on its own side. The deal record does not ship , , or mezzanine metadata the stitcher reads. AAMP buyer SDK flows still treat DSP activation as instructions, not as a guaranteed fetch of servable XML. Success in that layer means the seller agent accepted terms, trust gates cleared, and your orchestrator got a complete status. It does not mean an InLine resolved, wrappers terminated, or HTTPS media matched what the buy assumed. The agentic buying and OpenRTB stack map shows where negotiation sits relative to the bid stream. Negotiation moved up; the delivery contract did not shrink. What the VAST side still has to prove Whether the path is programmatic guaranteed, a PMP auction that returns bid.adm , or a direct ad-server handoff, the stitcher or player parses XML. For video it cares about: Duration versus the pod or break length sold. MediaFiles with codecs, bitrates, and HTTPS URLs the environment allows. Wrapper chains that end in an InLine before the SSAI deadline. Mezzanine and identity fields on paths that transcode from a master, not from the progressive MP4 in the first MediaFile . Suppose the agentic buy committed a fifteen-second CTV spot. The Deals Library shows success. The only creative pointer is: version = "4.2" > https://ads.example/vast?id=PG-8842 00:01:30 Schema validators may accept the wrapper. The break still rejects the ad: duration on the wrapper does not substitute for InLine truth, and nobody followed VASTAdTagURI to see whether the inner creative is fifteen seconds or ninety. OpenRTB can sit between the deal and the tag. When it does, the exchange still reads JSON on the forward hop. Field-level drift on imp.video or a missing pmp.deals entry is a sibling failure mode to an empty tag; the bid request object reference is the shape partners enforce before your seat ever sees a VAST URL. After the win, bid.adm or the ad-server redirect is yet another object again. Same flight, two verdicts Side What “done” means to operators What production still checks AAMP / Deals Library Seller accepted, task complete, deal id recorded SDK status, deal sync acknowledgment OpenRTB forward Request parses for the partner snapshot Deal id on imp.pmp.deals , duration bounds, AdCOM plcmt VAST delivery Player or SSAI can schedule the break Fetch XML, wrapper depth, media URLs, duration vs pod An integration can pass JSON Schema on the deal push and on a templated bid request while the tag URL 404s, loops wrappers, or serves HTTP media into a secure: 1 imp. Both JSON layers look fine in a dashboard. Fill dies at the stitcher. Prebid Server and other exchange edges are where many agentic forwards land. Their expectations for video imps and deal ids are documented per integration, not inside AAMP task objects. The Prebid Server exchange notes are a practical checklist for whether the OpenRTB hop matches what the auction module will actually route before anyone opens VAST. When the creative arrives inside the bid, bid.adm still has to be VAST XML, not a macro-expanded hope. The OpenRTB bid object fields describe what downstream parsers read after seatbid clears. How you catch it Split the check the way the stack splits objects. Auction hop: Run the forwarded bid request through rtblint ( cargo install rtblint , npm install rtblint-core , MCP rtblint-mcp ) against the dated OpenRTB snapshot your exchange partner enforces. Diff imp.pmp.deals , duration windows, and AdCOM video enums against the deal record the AAMP task wrote. An LLM implementing AdCP, ARTF, or AAMP output can emit plausible JSON and still get an OK from a stub validator. Creative hop: Paste the live tag URL or bid.adm into the VAST tag tester for fetch, preview, and tracking URLs. Run the same URL through the VAST inspector to resolve wrapper hops through to the InLine. vastlint ( cargo install vastlint , npm install vastlint ) owns that envelope. An implementation that lets a model emit the payload still has to check it on the wire. rtblint , vastlint , and pixellint are independent packages for OpenRTB, VAST, and pixel strings respectively. They are independent of IAB Tech Lab and of AAO; the specs do not require them. Wire both checks into the agent loop where you can: validate the bid request before forward, fetch and walk the tag before you mark the flight live. Where to go next Agentic buying and OpenRTB for how AAMP layers map onto execution specs. Version negotiation gaps on agentic OpenRTB when the partner snapshot and the agent template disagree. Will agents replace OpenRTB? on why the bid stream stays the floor under agentic negotiation.

On 13 November 2025, IAB Tech Lab released Agentic Real Time Framework (ARTF) v1.0 for public comment. The press release frames containerized agents sitting beside OpenRTB inside the same data center, not replacing the auction object underneath. Trade coverage situates that work inside the wider AAMP umbrella: negotiate and enrich upstairs, still transact on familiar rails.

If you run SSAI, a CTV ad server, or a DSP seat, the rail that actually schedules the break is still VAST. The buyer agent can return success long before anyone proves that XML exists.

What the AAMP side calls a finished video buy

Agentic Advertising Management Protocols (AAMP) stack agent interfaces on top of OpenDirect, the Deals API, AdCOM, OpenRTB, and VAST. On the buyer path, a programmatic video line often ends with three artifacts that look like delivery:

  1. A task status and a row in Agentic Deals or your Deals Library.
  2. A Deals API push (Deal Sync) with adtypes including video, floors, flight dates, and sometimes activation copy aimed at legacy DSP UIs.
  3. A VAST endpoint URL or activation_instructions text that tells a human to paste a deal id into a platform console.

None of those is the creative envelope. The IAB Deals API spec is explicit that the receiver must still validate every bid request that carries the deal id and must apply targeting on its own side. The deal record does not ship , , or mezzanine metadata the stitcher reads.

AAMP buyer SDK flows still treat DSP activation as instructions, not as a guaranteed fetch of servable XML. Success in that layer means the seller agent accepted terms, trust gates cleared, and your orchestrator got a complete status. It does not mean an InLine resolved, wrappers terminated, or HTTPS media matched what the buy assumed.

The agentic buying and OpenRTB stack map shows where negotiation sits relative to the bid stream. Negotiation moved up; the delivery contract did not shrink.

What the VAST side still has to prove

Whether the path is programmatic guaranteed, a PMP auction that returns bid.adm, or a direct ad-server handoff, the stitcher or player parses XML. For video it cares about:

  • Duration versus the pod or break length sold.
  • MediaFiles with codecs, bitrates, and HTTPS URLs the environment allows.
  • Wrapper chains that end in an InLine before the SSAI deadline.
  • Mezzanine and identity fields on paths that transcode from a master, not from the progressive MP4 in the first MediaFile.

Suppose the agentic buy committed a fifteen-second CTV spot. The Deals Library shows success. The only creative pointer is:

      00:01:30

Schema validators may accept the wrapper. The break still rejects the ad: duration on the wrapper does not substitute for InLine truth, and nobody followed VASTAdTagURI to see whether the inner creative is fifteen seconds or ninety.

OpenRTB can sit between the deal and the tag. When it does, the exchange still reads JSON on the forward hop. Field-level drift on imp.video or a missing pmp.deals entry is a sibling failure mode to an empty tag; the bid request object reference is the shape partners enforce before your seat ever sees a VAST URL. After the win, bid.adm or the ad-server redirect is yet another object again.

Same flight, two verdicts
Side What “done” means to operators What production still checks AAMP / Deals Library Seller accepted, task complete, deal id recorded SDK status, deal sync acknowledgment OpenRTB forward Request parses for the partner snapshot Deal id on imp.pmp.deals, duration bounds, AdCOM plcmt VAST delivery Player or SSAI can schedule the break Fetch XML, wrapper depth, media URLs, duration vs pod

An integration can pass JSON Schema on the deal push and on a templated bid request while the tag URL 404s, loops wrappers, or serves HTTP media into a secure: 1 imp. Both JSON layers look fine in a dashboard. Fill dies at the stitcher.

Prebid Server and other exchange edges are where many agentic forwards land. Their expectations for video imps and deal ids are documented per integration, not inside AAMP task objects. The Prebid Server exchange notes are a practical checklist for whether the OpenRTB hop matches what the auction module will actually route before anyone opens VAST.

When the creative arrives inside the bid, bid.adm still has to be VAST XML, not a macro-expanded hope. The OpenRTB bid object fields describe what downstream parsers read after seatbid clears.

How you catch it

Split the check the way the stack splits objects.

Auction hop: Run the forwarded bid request through rtblint (cargo install rtblint, npm install rtblint-core, MCP rtblint-mcp) against the dated OpenRTB snapshot your exchange partner enforces. Diff imp.pmp.deals, duration windows, and AdCOM video enums against the deal record the AAMP task wrote. An LLM implementing AdCP, ARTF, or AAMP output can emit plausible JSON and still get an OK from a stub validator.

Creative hop: Paste the live tag URL or bid.adm into the VAST tag tester for fetch, preview, and tracking URLs. Run the same URL through the VAST inspector to resolve wrapper hops through to the InLine. vastlint (cargo install vastlint, npm install vastlint) owns that envelope.

An implementation that lets a model emit the payload still has to check it on the wire. rtblint, vastlint, and pixellint are independent packages for OpenRTB, VAST, and pixel strings respectively. They are independent of IAB Tech Lab and of AAO; the specs do not require them.

Wire both checks into the agent loop where you can: validate the bid request before forward, fetch and walk the tag before you mark the flight live.

items.title: An AI Just Designed a Better Way to Break Your Keys
items.summary: An AI Just Designed a Better Way to Break Your Keys On October 16, Anthropic published something that should have made every cryptography engineer stop scrolling. Its model Claude Mythos 5, working in a closed loop with an automated evaluator, designed quantum circuits that beat the best published designs on seven out of eight tasks. One of those tasks was adding two points on an elliptic curve. That is the core step of Shor's attack on the elliptic-curve keys that protect Bitcoin wallets, Ethereum accounts, and a good share of the encrypted messaging on your phone. The headline number travelled fast: 17 times fewer gates. Social posts turned it into "AI designs quantum circuits 17 times more efficient than humans, in 53 hours, with no human help." Each part of that sentence is a little off, and the real story is more interesting than the viral version. What actually happened The work came out of Anthropic's STEM Fellows Program, led by Andi Gu with Alek Kemeny of Anthropic and Susanne Yelin and Mikhail Lukin of Harvard (Lukin also works with QuEra Computing). The preprint, "Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models," went up on arXiv on October 15 as arXiv:2610.22367. It has not been peer reviewed. The setup was simple in outline and careful in practice. Claude was given plain-language specifications for eight computational building blocks drawn from chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing. It wrote Python programs that generate circuits. An independent evaluator checked each proposed circuit for correctness and scored it on a combined cost: Toffoli gate count multiplied by peak qubit count. Good designs survived in an evolutionary search built on the open-source tool OpenEvolve, and good ideas crossed between approaches. In seven of the eight tasks, the circuits Claude found used both fewer gates and fewer qubits than the published best. The largest gain, on a fixed-point Gaussian task, was 39 times on the combined cost metric. The eighth task, elliptic-curve point addition, is the one that matters for cryptography, and it is also the one where the numbers need the most care. The 17x, explained honestly Point addition dominates the cost of a quantum attack on elliptic-curve keys, and modular inversion accounts for most of point addition. Classical computers handle inversion efficiently with a method called divsteps, but a straightforward quantum version has to store a record of every branch it takes, which costs many extra qubits. In one 53-hour run with minimal human input, Claude found a rule that recovers that record from the numbers themselves. The team tested it in large numerical simulations and formalized it in the Lean proof assistant: the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history. From that, Claude built a family of designs that trade qubits for gates. One design uses about 12 percent more qubits than the smallest previous design and 17 times fewer Toffoli gates. The benchmark curve is secp256k1, the curve Bitcoin uses. Another design in the same family goes the other direction: 12 times fewer Toffoli gates than the previous best, from 5.1 million down to about 440,000, while also using fewer qubits. So the 17x is real, and it is also one comparison on one task, against one earlier design, for 12 percent more qubits. It is a circuit-resource claim about published constructions, not a statement that cryptography is broken or that Bitcoin is at risk. None of these circuits has run on quantum hardware. Every check was a classical simulation, an automated evaluator, or a formal proof. There is no machine that can run them yet, and the paper says nothing about when one will exist. Anthropic is also open about a detail the viral posts skipped: Claude was, in their words, "conservative by nature." It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements and sometimes double- and triple-checked results that were already well supported. The loop needed occasional prompts to think more broadly. This was not a model left alone in a room for two days. It was a model inside a well-built search harness, with humans setting the task and the scoring. None of that makes the result unimportant. It makes it a result instead of a myth, and the result is still worth sitting with. Why this one is different from the last ten quantum warnings I have written before about resource estimates for breaking RSA and elliptic-curve keys falling. In late October, Alice & Bob estimated 22,593 physical qubits to factor RSA-2048 in about three days, 40 times fewer than Google's 2025 estimate. IonQ put the elliptic-curve problem at 19,397 trapped-ion qubits. Those were improvements in hardware assumptions and in how cleverly humans compile Shor's algorithm. This is a different kind of improvement. The bottleneck in those estimates has always been human cleverness: someone has to find a smarter circuit, a better error-correcting code, a tighter compilation. Now a general-purpose AI model, given a verifier and a scoring function, found a smarter circuit on its own, in a weekend, on a problem humans have been optimizing for years. The search that produced it was not even aimed at cryptography. Point addition was one of eight tasks, and the model improved seven of them. That is the part that changes the shape of the timeline. Hardware progress is slow and visible: you can count qubits in a lab. Algorithmic progress is quiet until it is published, and now one of its sources is a system that can run thousands of experiments without getting tired. The estimates of what a future machine needs will keep falling, and the rate at which they fall is no longer set only by how many clever humans work on the problem. I want to be careful here, because I dislike hype as much as anyone. This paper does not move the date a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives. It does not change the fact that the best machines in service today have around a hundred qubits and the estimates need tens of thousands. What it changes is the confidence you should have in any timeline that assumes the attack side stays at its current level of cleverness. It will not. What it means if you build things If you are building a messenger, a wallet, a VPN, or anything that encrypts data meant to stay private for years, the practical conclusion has not changed, but the margin for delay has shrunk again. Harvest now, decrypt later is the threat that makes all of this concrete. An attacker does not need a quantum computer today. They need to record your encrypted traffic today and keep it until a machine exists that can break it. Anything encrypted with a static elliptic-curve or RSA key, stored backups, signed documents, archived messages, is exposed to a machine that might arrive in the 2030s. Session keys protected by forward secrecy limit the damage for live conversations. Long-lived data gets no such protection. So the work is the same work it has been for two years, just more urgent: Migrate key exchange and signatures to the NIST standards, ML-KEM for key encapsulation and ML-DSA for signatures, and do it in hybrid form alongside the classical algorithms while the ecosystem catches up. That is what I did in my own messenger: the handshake now runs ML-KEM-768 next to ECDH P-256, and identity keys are ML-DSA-65. The hybrid part matters. The new standards are young, and if something turns out to be wrong with one of them, the classical half still holds. The sizes are annoying, ML-DSA signatures are thousands of bytes where an ECDSA signature is 64, and you will feel that in every protocol that was designed around small keys. You feel it once, during the migration. You do not get to choose when the attacker feels it. Build crypto-agility in from the start, not as a refactor later. If your code assumes one algorithm in one place, swapping it is a rewrite. If your key bundles carry an algorithm identifier and your handshake negotiates, swapping it is a version bump. I learned this the slow way, by having to touch every place a key was serialized. The second migration is always cheaper than the first, but only if the first one leaves room for it. And treat every new resource estimate as a data point, not a deadline. The honest timeline for a machine that breaks RSA-2048 is still "sometime in the 2030s, maybe, if several hard problems get solved." An AI Just Designed a Better Way to Break Your Keys

On October 16, Anthropic published something that should have made every cryptography engineer stop scrolling. Its model Claude Mythos 5, working in a closed loop with an automated evaluator, designed quantum circuits that beat the best published designs on seven out of eight tasks. One of those tasks was adding two points on an elliptic curve. That is the core step of Shor's attack on the elliptic-curve keys that protect Bitcoin wallets, Ethereum accounts, and a good share of the encrypted messaging on your phone.

The headline number travelled fast: 17 times fewer gates. Social posts turned it into "AI designs quantum circuits 17 times more efficient than humans, in 53 hours, with no human help." Each part of that sentence is a little off, and the real story is more interesting than the viral version.

What actually happened

The work came out of Anthropic's STEM Fellows Program, led by Andi Gu with Alek Kemeny of Anthropic and Susanne Yelin and Mikhail Lukin of Harvard (Lukin also works with QuEra Computing). The preprint, "Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models," went up on arXiv on October 15 as arXiv:2610.22367. It has not been peer reviewed.

The setup was simple in outline and careful in practice. Claude was given plain-language specifications for eight computational building blocks drawn from chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing. It wrote Python programs that generate circuits. An independent evaluator checked each proposed circuit for correctness and scored it on a combined cost: Toffoli gate count multiplied by peak qubit count. Good designs survived in an evolutionary search built on the open-source tool OpenEvolve, and good ideas crossed between approaches.

In seven of the eight tasks, the circuits Claude found used both fewer gates and fewer qubits than the published best. The largest gain, on a fixed-point Gaussian task, was 39 times on the combined cost metric. The eighth task, elliptic-curve point addition, is the one that matters for cryptography, and it is also the one where the numbers need the most care.

The 17x, explained honestly

Point addition dominates the cost of a quantum attack on elliptic-curve keys, and modular inversion accounts for most of point addition. Classical computers handle inversion efficiently with a method called divsteps, but a straightforward quantum version has to store a record of every branch it takes, which costs many extra qubits. In one 53-hour run with minimal human input, Claude found a rule that recovers that record from the numbers themselves. The team tested it in large numerical simulations and formalized it in the Lean proof assistant: the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history.

From that, Claude built a family of designs that trade qubits for gates. One design uses about 12 percent more qubits than the smallest previous design and 17 times fewer Toffoli gates. The benchmark curve is secp256k1, the curve Bitcoin uses. Another design in the same family goes the other direction: 12 times fewer Toffoli gates than the previous best, from 5.1 million down to about 440,000, while also using fewer qubits.

So the 17x is real, and it is also one comparison on one task, against one earlier design, for 12 percent more qubits. It is a circuit-resource claim about published constructions, not a statement that cryptography is broken or that Bitcoin is at risk. None of these circuits has run on quantum hardware. Every check was a classical simulation, an automated evaluator, or a formal proof. There is no machine that can run them yet, and the paper says nothing about when one will exist.

Anthropic is also open about a detail the viral posts skipped: Claude was, in their words, "conservative by nature." It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements and sometimes double- and triple-checked results that were already well supported. The loop needed occasional prompts to think more broadly. This was not a model left alone in a room for two days. It was a model inside a well-built search harness, with humans setting the task and the scoring.

None of that makes the result unimportant. It makes it a result instead of a myth, and the result is still worth sitting with.

Why this one is different from the last ten quantum warnings

I have written before about resource estimates for breaking RSA and elliptic-curve keys falling. In late October, Alice & Bob estimated 22,593 physical qubits to factor RSA-2048 in about three days, 40 times fewer than Google's 2025 estimate. IonQ put the elliptic-curve problem at 19,397 trapped-ion qubits. Those were improvements in hardware assumptions and in how cleverly humans compile Shor's algorithm.

This is a different kind of improvement. The bottleneck in those estimates has always been human cleverness: someone has to find a smarter circuit, a better error-correcting code, a tighter compilation. Now a general-purpose AI model, given a verifier and a scoring function, found a smarter circuit on its own, in a weekend, on a problem humans have been optimizing for years. The search that produced it was not even aimed at cryptography. Point addition was one of eight tasks, and the model improved seven of them.

That is the part that changes the shape of the timeline. Hardware progress is slow and visible: you can count qubits in a lab. Algorithmic progress is quiet until it is published, and now one of its sources is a system that can run thousands of experiments without getting tired. The estimates of what a future machine needs will keep falling, and the rate at which they fall is no longer set only by how many clever humans work on the problem.

I want to be careful here, because I dislike hype as much as anyone. This paper does not move the date a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives. It does not change the fact that the best machines in service today have around a hundred qubits and the estimates need tens of thousands. What it changes is the confidence you should have in any timeline that assumes the attack side stays at its current level of cleverness. It will not.

What it means if you build things

If you are building a messenger, a wallet, a VPN, or anything that encrypts data meant to stay private for years, the practical conclusion has not changed, but the margin for delay has shrunk again.

Harvest now, decrypt later is the threat that makes all of this concrete. An attacker does not need a quantum computer today. They need to record your encrypted traffic today and keep it until a machine exists that can break it. Anything encrypted with a static elliptic-curve or RSA key, stored backups, signed documents, archived messages, is exposed to a machine that might arrive in the 2030s. Session keys protected by forward secrecy limit the damage for live conversations. Long-lived data gets no such protection.

So the work is the same work it has been for two years, just more urgent:

Migrate key exchange and signatures to the NIST standards, ML-KEM for key encapsulation and ML-DSA for signatures, and do it in hybrid form alongside the classical algorithms while the ecosystem catches up. That is what I did in my own messenger: the handshake now runs ML-KEM-768 next to ECDH P-256, and identity keys are ML-DSA-65. The hybrid part matters. The new standards are young, and if something turns out to be wrong with one of them, the classical half still holds. The sizes are annoying, ML-DSA signatures are thousands of bytes where an ECDSA signature is 64, and you will feel that in every protocol that was designed around small keys. You feel it once, during the migration. You do not get to choose when the attacker feels it.

Build crypto-agility in from the start, not as a refactor later. If your code assumes one algorithm in one place, swapping it is a rewrite. If your key bundles carry an algorithm identifier and your handshake negotiates, swapping it is a version bump. I learned this the slow way, by having to touch every place a key was serialized. The second migration is always cheaper than the first, but only if the first one leaves room for it.

DEVNULL , timeout = 4 , ) except ( OSError , subprocess . SubprocessError ) : return subprocess . A parent session can look clean while a subagent leaves trailing whitespace, conflict markers, or a half-finished edit in the tree. A SubagentStop hook runs when the subagent finishes, so you can refuse the handoff until git diff --check is clean.

The hook should name the problem and exit 2.

The hook

Save this as .claude/hooks/subagent_stop_check.py and make it executable:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import subprocess
import sys

def git(*args: str) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess[str]:
    try:
        return subprocess.run(
            ["git", *args],
            text=True,
            stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
            stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL,
            timeout=4,
        )
    except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError):
        return subprocess.CompletedProcess(args=["git", *args], returncode=0, stdout="", stderr="")

inside = git("rev-parse", "--is-inside-work-tree")
if inside.returncode != 0 or inside.stdout.strip() != "true":
    sys.exit(0)

check = git("diff", "--check")
if check.returncode != 0:
    print("SubagentStop: git diff --check failed. Fix whitespace or conflict markers before merging the handoff.")
    sys.exit(2)

status = git("status", "--porcelain")
paths = [line for line in (status.stdout or "").splitlines() if line.strip()]
print(f"SubagentStop: {len(paths)} changed path(s). Verify assumptions, tests, and secret boundaries before merging the handoff.")

Wire it in .claude/settings.json under SubagentStop with command set to python3 .claude/hooks/subagent_stop_check.py.

Why this beats a pasted prompt

Hooks run on the event, not when you remember to say "check the subagent's diff." The parent transcript is a poor place to notice a whitespace error or a conflict marker the subagent left behind. If the hook fires, fix the tree in the subagent's work or in a follow-up edit; do not merge the handoff and hope a later review catches it.

Tips
  • Keep the hook local, fast, and free of network calls.
  • Pair it with a Stop hook that refuses "done" while the build or tests are still red, so both the subagent handoff and the parent turn have a mechanical check.
  • If a generated file trips git diff --check, fix or exclude that path rather than deleting the hook.

items.title: Large AI-Generated Property Images in Node.js — Tenant-Private Multipart Boundaries
items.summary: Short answer: for tenant-scoped property exports, authorize an immutable image manifest before reading object bytes, keep the bucket private, and use multipart only when a large generated image can be replayed in independent ranges. The upload method matters, but the production boundary is the manifest that proves every object belongs to the requesting tenant. The page fires because an export candidate references an object outside its tenant scope. On-call sees an export ID, a tenant-safe identifier, and the rejected object version; it does not see a vague “upload failed” message. Stop that export. Don't turn an ownership rejection into a retry storm. I've been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. Those incidents train a useful reflex: work backward from the tenant-visible action, not forward from whichever queue happens to look suspicious. For this system, the investigation path is export manifest, image record, generation job, then transfer attempt. Upload latency is supporting evidence. Authorization is the decision. Failure trace: the tenant-scoped export rejects an object A private bucket prevents anonymous reads; it does not prove that tenant A may receive an object stored for tenant B. That proof belongs in application data and policy. Each generated property image needs a tenant ID, property ID, immutable object key, object version, expected byte count, checksum evidence, generation job ID, and readiness state. The export worker must select the record by tenant and image identity together, then carry the authorized version into the manifest. This makes the alert actionable. A responder can distinguish three conditions that otherwise collapse into “missing image”: the image is still transferring, the image is complete but absent from the authorized manifest, or the manifest contains an ownership mismatch. Only the first is an upload-progress problem. The second is a workflow join problem. The third is a security boundary and should fail closed. No blind retry. The object key may include a tenant prefix for operations and lifecycle management, but a prefix is not authority. Queue payloads, filenames, and caller-provided paths are inputs. The database lookup and export authorization decision establish ownership. A duplicate generation delivery should converge on the same transfer attempt when it represents the same logical image, while an intentional regeneration should allocate a new immutable version so an export never changes underneath a reader. The earlier signal should therefore fire at manifest construction. Count rejected candidates by reason, record a structured audit event, and stop before any storage read. Keep tenant and object identifiers in access-controlled logs or traces rather than metric labels; counters can use bounded reasons such as tenant_mismatch , not_ready , and version_mismatch . This moves detection from a tenant-visible archive to the first place the service has enough information to prove the join is wrong. Upload decision: how should Node.js send large AI-generated files to private object storage? Choose the least complex transfer that meets the recovery requirement. A single streaming request is the default for an image that can be resent cheaply. Multipart earns its extra state when the generated file is large enough that repeating the whole transfer is operationally painful and the source can replay byte ranges. Amazon S3 defines multipart upload as three operations: initiate the upload, upload parts, and complete it. Parts can be uploaded independently and retransmitted after a failure. Its documented limits allow up to 10,000 parts, and every part except the last must be at least 5 MiB. Treat those as service-specific limits, not universal object-storage law; verify the contract of the implementation you deploy. Part size is a recovery boundary. Larger parts create fewer requests and repeat more bytes when one part must be sent again. Smaller parts narrow each retry but increase bookkeeping. I'm not sure there is a useful global default for AI-generated property images because the answer depends on the actual size distribution, source replay behavior, worker memory ceiling, and request limits. Measure those inputs, then keep the threshold and concurrency configurable. Node.js should apply backpressure from the storage writer to the image source and bound concurrency both per object and per worker process. Persist the multipart upload ID and each accepted part result before acknowledging queue progress. Completion is a separate state transition: an HTTP success for one part cannot make an image eligible for export, because the multipart operation has not yet assembled the object. The export manifest accepts only the immutable version marked ready after completion and verification. Transfer shape Recovery unit Isolation requirement Operational fit Single streaming upload Entire object Authorize the reserved key and final version Smaller images or sources that cannot replay ranges Multipart upload One replayable part Bind upload ID, key, and parts to one tenant record Large images where partial retry offsets added state Managed media pipeline Provider-defined job Preserve tenant identity across its job and delivery model Teams prioritizing transformations over transfer control Multipart isn't suitable when the producer cannot reproduce an exact byte range, images are routinely small, or the team cannot own abandoned-upload cleanup and reconciliation. Stick with one streaming upload in those cases. A managed media pipeline can be the better boundary when resizing, format conversion, and delivery policy dominate the problem; direct object storage gives the application finer control over the tenant manifest, with more state for the team to operate. Security boundary: authorize the export manifest before fetching bytes Manifest construction is where the property-management scenario becomes concrete. Suppose tenant tenant-17 requests a ZIP export of listing photos. The query must return only records scoped to tenant-17 , but the worker still validates every row before it asks storage for bytes. Defense in depth here is cheap compared with explaining a cross-tenant archive. The gate below is deliberately boring. It does not know how bytes were uploaded, and it does not accept an object-key prefix as proof. It checks the authorized tenant, immutable version, readiness, expected size, and checksum decision that the upload workflow already recorded. package exportmanifest import ( "errors" "fmt" ) type ImageRecord struct { TenantID string ObjectKey string ObjectVersion string State string ExpectedBytes int64 StoredBytes int64 ChecksumOK bool } type ManifestItem struct { ObjectKey string ObjectVersion string } func Authorize ( record ImageRecord , requestedTenant string ) ( ManifestItem , error ) { if requestedTenant == "" || record . TenantID != requestedTenant { return ManifestItem { } , errors . New ( "tenant scope mismatch" ) } if record . ObjectKey == "" || record . ObjectVersion == "" { return ManifestItem { } , errors . New ( "immutable object identity is missing" ) } if record . State != "ready" { return ManifestItem { } , fmt . Errorf ( "image state is %q" , record . State ) } if record . StoredBytes != record . ExpectedBytes || ! record . ChecksumOK { return ManifestItem { } , errors . New ( "object completeness is unverified" ) } return ManifestItem { ObjectKey : record . ObjectKey , ObjectVersion : record . ObjectVersion , } , nil } Keep transfer retry logic elsewhere. Mixing it into the export gate makes an authorization failure look recoverable and invites a dangerous behavior: retrying with a newly resolved record that was never part of the approved manifest. The export worker should consume a frozen list of authorized object versions. If any item fails validation or reading, fail the export and rebuild a fresh manifest through the same tenant-scoped path. Crash points deserve explicit tests because the queue's delivery contract and the storage operation do not share a transaction. Terminate a worker after a part result is stored, redeliver the same generation message twice, and verify that a replacement resumes the same tenant-bound attempt without creating two ready versions. Then terminate after object completion but before the application marks the image ready; reconciliation should verify the recorded identity and completeness before advancing the existing record. Finally, build a tenant tenant-17 export with one deliberately injected tenant-29 record and prove that the manifest gate rejects it before a storage read. That last test is the important one. Verification: move the first signal to the workflow join The late page tells on-call that an export was blocked. The earlier signal should show why the manifest population is drifting before an export deadline is threatened. Instrument state transitions for generation allocated, transfer active, object ready, manifest accepted, and export complete. Observe completion latency by object-size band, age of the oldest nonterminal transfer, repeated part bytes, manifest rejection reasons, and exports waiting on images. Use bounded dimensions. Tenant ID, object key, upload ID, and export ID belong in correlated logs and traces where access is controlled; putting them into metric labels creates an unbounded operational surface. An alert can link to the relevant trace using a tenant-safe correlation value without turning the metrics system into an object index. The runbook starts at the rejected manifest item. Confirm the requested tenant and immutable version, inspect the image record's last state transition, then follow its generation and transfer correlation IDs. If the record is not ready, the transfer owner handles it. If it is ready but missing from the manifest, inspect the tenant-scoped join. If ownership differs, preserve the audit evidence and keep the export closed. These are separate actions, so they need separate reason codes and separate alert routing. Roll out the instrumentation before tightening the page, then watch it through normal generation bursts and scheduled tenant exports. Your mileage may vary, especially when a portfolio imports many property photos at once; the useful threshold is tied to export risk, not a fashionable latency percentile. False-positive cost: set the threshold by tenant-visible risk Page when an unresolved state threatens a scheduled export or when the manifest gate observes an ownership mismatch. Queue a ticket or automated cleanup for an old multipart attempt that blocks no export. This split keeps on-call focused while still closing incomplete multipart uploads under the storage service's documented lifecycle. The catch is sensitivity. A threshold based only on elapsed upload age will page during legitimate large transfers, while a threshold based only on queue depth can miss one stuck high-priority export. Combine lack of state progress with an approaching export deadline, and route ownership rejection separately because its response is to stop and inspect, not to transfer faster. Too loose, and the tenant discovers the problem. Too tight, and responders learn to distrust the page. Both are failures. False positives have a real reliability cost: they interrupt investigation, encourage broad retries, and hide the rare authorization signal among ordinary slow transfers. Start with audit-only measurements, rehearse the three failure points above, and promote a condition to paging only when the runbook names a concrete decision. The correct upload strategy leaves on-call with one tenant-bound record, one immutable object version, and one clear action. Short answer: for tenant-scoped property exports, authorize an immutable image manifest before reading object bytes, keep the bucket private, and use multipart only when a large generated image can be replayed in independent ranges. The upload method matters, but the production boundary is the manifest that proves every object belongs to the requesting tenant.

The page fires because an export candidate references an object outside its tenant scope. On-call sees an export ID, a tenant-safe identifier, and the rejected object version; it does not see a vague “upload failed” message. Stop that export. Don't turn an ownership rejection into a retry storm.

I've been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. Those incidents train a useful reflex: work backward from the tenant-visible action, not forward from whichever queue happens to look suspicious. For this system, the investigation path is export manifest, image record, generation job, then transfer attempt. Upload latency is supporting evidence. Authorization is the decision.

Failure trace: the tenant-scoped export rejects an object

A private bucket prevents anonymous reads; it does not prove that tenant A may receive an object stored for tenant B. That proof belongs in application data and policy. Each generated property image needs a tenant ID, property ID, immutable object key, object version, expected byte count, checksum evidence, generation job ID, and readiness state. The export worker must select the record by tenant and image identity together, then carry the authorized version into the manifest.

This makes the alert actionable. A responder can distinguish three conditions that otherwise collapse into “missing image”: the image is still transferring, the image is complete but absent from the authorized manifest, or the manifest contains an ownership mismatch. Only the first is an upload-progress problem. The second is a workflow join problem. The third is a security boundary and should fail closed.

No blind retry.

The object key may include a tenant prefix for operations and lifecycle management, but a prefix is not authority. Queue payloads, filenames, and caller-provided paths are inputs. The database lookup and export authorization decision establish ownership. A duplicate generation delivery should converge on the same transfer attempt when it represents the same logical image, while an intentional regeneration should allocate a new immutable version so an export never changes underneath a reader.

The earlier signal should therefore fire at manifest construction. Count rejected candidates by reason, record a structured audit event, and stop before any storage read. Keep tenant and object identifiers in access-controlled logs or traces rather than metric labels; counters can use bounded reasons such as tenant_mismatch, not_ready, and version_mismatch. This moves detection from a tenant-visible archive to the first place the service has enough information to prove the join is wrong.

Upload decision: how should Node.js send large AI-generated files to private object storage?

Choose the least complex transfer that meets the recovery requirement. A single streaming request is the default for an image that can be resent cheaply. Multipart earns its extra state when the generated file is large enough that repeating the whole transfer is operationally painful and the source can replay byte ranges.

Amazon S3 defines multipart upload as three operations: initiate the upload, upload parts, and complete it. Parts can be uploaded independently and retransmitted after a failure. Its documented limits allow up to 10,000 parts, and every part except the last must be at least 5 MiB. Treat those as service-specific limits, not universal object-storage law; verify the contract of the implementation you deploy.

Part size is a recovery boundary. Larger parts create fewer requests and repeat more bytes when one part must be sent again. Smaller parts narrow each retry but increase bookkeeping. I'm not sure there is a useful global default for AI-generated property images because the answer depends on the actual size distribution, source replay behavior, worker memory ceiling, and request limits. Measure those inputs, then keep the threshold and concurrency configurable.

Node.js should apply backpressure from the storage writer to the image source and bound concurrency both per object and per worker process. Persist the multipart upload ID and each accepted part result before acknowledging queue progress. Completion is a separate state transition: an HTTP success for one part cannot make an image eligible for export, because the multipart operation has not yet assembled the object. The export manifest accepts only the immutable version marked ready after completion and verification.

Transfer shape Recovery unit Isolation requirement Operational fit Single streaming upload Entire object Authorize the reserved key and final version Smaller images or sources that cannot replay ranges Multipart upload One replayable part Bind upload ID, key, and parts to one tenant record Large images where partial retry offsets added state Managed media pipeline Provider-defined job Preserve tenant identity across its job and delivery model Teams prioritizing transformations over transfer control

Multipart isn't suitable when the producer cannot reproduce an exact byte range, images are routinely small, or the team cannot own abandoned-upload cleanup and reconciliation. Stick with one streaming upload in those cases. A managed media pipeline can be the better boundary when resizing, format conversion, and delivery policy dominate the problem; direct object storage gives the application finer control over the tenant manifest, with more state for the team to operate.

Security boundary: authorize the export manifest before fetching bytes

Manifest construction is where the property-management scenario becomes concrete. Suppose tenant tenant-17 requests a ZIP export of listing photos. The query must return only records scoped to tenant-17, but the worker still validates every row before it asks storage for bytes. Defense in depth here is cheap compared with explaining a cross-tenant archive.

The gate below is deliberately boring. It does not know how bytes were uploaded, and it does not accept an object-key prefix as proof. It checks the authorized tenant, immutable version, readiness, expected size, and checksum decision that the upload workflow already recorded.

package exportmanifest

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

type ImageRecord struct {
    TenantID      string
    ObjectKey     string
    ObjectVersion string
    State         string
    ExpectedBytes int64
    StoredBytes   int64
    ChecksumOK    bool
}

type ManifestItem struct {
    ObjectKey     string
    ObjectVersion string
}

func Authorize(record ImageRecord, requestedTenant string) (ManifestItem, error) {
    if requestedTenant == "" || record.TenantID != requestedTenant {
        return ManifestItem{}, errors.New("tenant scope mismatch")
    }
    if record.ObjectKey == "" || record.ObjectVersion == "" {
        return ManifestItem{}, errors.New("immutable object identity is missing")
    }
    if record.State != "ready" {
        return ManifestItem{}, fmt.Errorf("image state is %q", record.State)
    }
    if record.StoredBytes != record.ExpectedBytes || !record.ChecksumOK {
        return ManifestItem{}, errors.New("object completeness is unverified")
    }

    return ManifestItem{
        ObjectKey:     record.ObjectKey,
        ObjectVersion: record.ObjectVersion,
    }, nil
}

Keep transfer retry logic elsewhere. Mixing it into the export gate makes an authorization failure look recoverable and invites a dangerous behavior: retrying with a newly resolved record that was never part of the approved manifest. The export worker should consume a frozen list of authorized object versions. If any item fails validation or reading, fail the export and rebuild a fresh manifest through the same tenant-scoped path.

Crash points deserve explicit tests because the queue's delivery contract and the storage operation do not share a transaction. Terminate a worker after a part result is stored, redeliver the same generation message twice, and verify that a replacement resumes the same tenant-bound attempt without creating two ready versions. Then terminate after object completion but before the application marks the image ready; reconciliation should verify the recorded identity and completeness before advancing the existing record. Finally, build a tenant tenant-17 export with one deliberately injected tenant-29 record and prove that the manifest gate rejects it before a storage read.

That last test is the important one.

Verification: move the first signal to the workflow join

The late page tells on-call that an export was blocked. The earlier signal should show why the manifest population is drifting before an export deadline is threatened. Instrument state transitions for generation allocated, transfer active, object ready, manifest accepted, and export complete. Observe completion latency by object-size band, age of the oldest nonterminal transfer, repeated part bytes, manifest rejection reasons, and exports waiting on images.

Use bounded dimensions. Tenant ID, object key, upload ID, and export ID belong in correlated logs and traces where access is controlled; putting them into metric labels creates an unbounded operational surface. An alert can link to the relevant trace using a tenant-safe correlation value without turning the metrics system into an object index.

The runbook starts at the rejected manifest item. Confirm the requested tenant and immutable version, inspect the image record's last state transition, then follow its generation and transfer correlation IDs. If the record is not ready, the transfer owner handles it. If it is ready but missing from the manifest, inspect the tenant-scoped join. If ownership differs, preserve the audit evidence and keep the export closed. These are separate actions, so they need separate reason codes and separate alert routing. Roll out the instrumentation before tightening the page, then watch it through normal generation bursts and scheduled tenant exports. Your mileage may vary, especially when a portfolio imports many property photos at once; the useful threshold is tied to export risk, not a fashionable latency percentile.

False-positive cost: set the threshold by tenant-visible risk

Page when an unresolved state threatens a scheduled export or when the manifest gate observes an ownership mismatch. Queue a ticket or automated cleanup for an old multipart attempt that blocks no export. This split keeps on-call focused while still closing incomplete multipart uploads under the storage service's documented lifecycle.

The catch is sensitivity. A threshold based only on elapsed upload age will page during legitimate large transfers, while a threshold based only on queue depth can miss one stuck high-priority export. Combine lack of state progress with an approaching export deadline, and route ownership rejection separately because its response is to stop and inspect, not to transfer faster.

Too loose, and the tenant discovers the problem. Too tight, and responders learn to distrust the page.

Both are failures.

False positives have a real reliability cost: they interrupt investigation, encourage broad retries, and hide the rare authorization signal among ordinary slow transfers. Start with audit-only measurements, rehearse the three failure points above, and promote a condition to paging only when the runbook names a concrete decision. The correct upload strategy leaves on-call with one tenant-bound record, one immutable object version, and one clear action.

  • https://cloudinary.com/documentation
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

items.title: I swept all 91 pages of my "Top 500" list. Rank #500 and rank #501 have identical data.
items.summary: I have a directory of AI tools — 4,323 listings, live at aiverse.mindutil.com — and I keep publishing posts about how the numbers on my own pages are produced. Yesterday it was the click counter. Today I went looking for the bottom of my own list, and found that it doesn't have one. The setup: two "browse everything" pages My site has three pages whose job is to enumerate the catalog: /ai-tools — the full directory, 24 cards per page, sorted by a mirrored read count /top-ai-tools — "🏆 Top AI Tools", 48 cards per page, sorted by rating /new-ai-tools — same grid, sorted by the publication date the upstream source gives me All three render a numbered rank badge on each card on /top-ai-tools (1, 2, 3 …), and the header on that page carries a pill that says "Top 500" . So: how many pages is that, really? /ai-tools last page linked: 181 (180 × 24 + 3 = 4,323) /top-ai-tools last page linked: 91 (90 × 48 + 3 = 4,323) /new-ai-tools last page linked: 181 The arithmetic is fine. I checked it: I fetched all 91 pages of /top-ai-tools and all the rank badges came out as a contiguous run, 1 … 4,323, no duplicates, no gaps , 4,323 distinct listings, exactly the row count of the table. Pagination integrity: passes. Then I asked for page 92. Past the last page, the site stops telling the truth GET /top-ai-tools?page=92 → HTTP 200 . Not a 404, not a redirect to page 91. It renders the same header, the same "🏆 Top AI Tools" title, a rel="prev" link back to page 91, and zero cards. GET /ai-tools?page=182 is worse, because that page still has a count in its intro copy: All AI Tools - Browse the Full Directory | AIVerse All AI Tools "Explore 4,323 curated AI tools. Use the filters to narrow down by category, pricing and rating." "4,323 tools found" "No tools match your current search and filters. Try removing some filters or searching for something else." rel = "canonical" href = "https://aiverse.mindutil.com/ai-tools?page=182" > name = "robots" content = "index, follow" > Same page, two contradictory sentences. The "4,323 tools found" line and the empty-state line come from different queries: the count is prisma.tool.count() over the filter (which ignores page ), the grid is findMany() with skip/take . Off the end of the list, the count stays at 4,323 and the grid goes empty. The copy layer never hears about the other one. And it's indexable, with a canonical that points at itself. Page 300: also 200. Page 999999: also 200, also index, follow . I tried six different out-of-range page numbers across four listings; every one answered 200 with robots: index, follow and a self-referencing canonical: URL status cards robots canonical /ai-tools?page=182 200 0 index, follow ?page=182 /ai-tools?page=300 200 0 index, follow ?page=300 /ai-tools?page=9999 200 0 index, follow ?page=9999 /ai-tools?page=1e9 200 0 index, follow …?page=1000000000 /top-ai-tools?page=92 200 0 index, follow ?page=92 /free-ai-tools?page=200 200 0 index, follow ?page=200 ?page=1e9 deserves its own line. The parser is: export function parsePage ( value : unknown ) : number { const n = Number ( Array . isArray ( value ) ? value [ 0 ] : value ) ; return Number . isFinite ( n ) && n >= 1 ? Math . floor ( n ) : 1 ; } Number("1e9") is finite and ≥ 1, so it becomes skip: 23999999976 . 0 , -1 and abc clamp to page 1 — those are handled; everything numeric just… keeps going. There's no upper bound because the handler doesn't know totalPages yet, and totalPages is computed inside the query it's supposed to guard. Why I care: this is not only a UX thing. A parameter that accepts unbounded integers and answers 200 + index is a crawl-budget question — it's how a site with 4,443 sitemap URLs ends up with an effectively unlimited set of indexable URLs. The fix is four lines (clamp to totalPages , or return 404 past the end, and canonical any clamped page to the real one). I haven't deployed it, because today's rule for this series was "measure, don't touch the code". The rank badge is a lie, but not in the way you'd expect Back to /top-ai-tools . The badge next to each card is a real ordinal — it went 1 to 4,323 with no repeats. The problem is what it's an ordinal of . The order is: case "rating" : return [ { rating : "desc" } , { ratingCount : "desc" } ] ; Across the whole 4,323-row sweep there are only 258 distinct (rating, ratingCount) pairs . Which means most of my ranking is not a ranking. rows whose (rating, ratingCount) pair is unique ........ 190 (4.4%) rows that share their pair with at least one other row . 4,133 (95.6%) biggest tie: (4.5, 2 reviews) = 695 rows, ranks 2,217–2,911 second: (5.0, 1 review) = 534 rows, ranks 222–755 695 listings are tied on both numbers at once, and I printed them as rank 2,217 through 2,911 in some order that is decided by the database's scan, not by anything I measured. Within a tie, SQLite gives whatever the scan gives — it's stable when the table doesn't change (I re-fetched page 50 twice, byte-identical), and undefined as a ranking. That directly breaks the "Top 500" pill in the header. The boundary falls inside the (5.0, 1 review) block: 279 rows with 5.0/1 review are inside the Top 500, 255 rows with exactly the same two numbers are outside it, and 497 of the first 500 rows share their numbers with another row. The cut line between "top" and "not top" runs through a tie. Nobody decided it; the offset did. The top of the list has its own problem. Rank 1 is Dall-E 2 with "Rated 6.3 out of 5" (3 reviews) — a rating that is arithmetically impossible on the scale the label claims, which comes from the same mirrored source as everything else, and which beats every 5.0 row precisely because rating: "desc" compares floats first. Rank 2 is Math99th at 5.0 with 28 reviews, tagged RIP AI — as are 83 of my first 500 rows. So the single highest-ranked tool on the site is an out-of-scale artifact, and the second is a product I've labeled as dead. At the other end, 129 rows have no rating at all and still got rank badges (4,195–4,323). What I'm taking away A count and a list from the same filter are two different queries, and "N tools found" above an empty grid is a bug I can now reproduce on demand. index, follow + self-canonical on unbounded page numbers is a crawl surface I created by not clamping a number. An ordinal badge is only a claim of order if the sort key actually separates rows. With 258 distinct keys over 4,323 rows, 95.6% of my rank numbers describe a tie. If a page says "Top 500", the boundary must be a decision (a threshold, or a documented tie-break), not an artifact of skip . The tie-break fix that costs nothing: append a stable unique key ( { id: "asc" } ) so at least the order is reproducible rather than merely usually-stable — and then stop printing 4,323 rank numbers for 258 distinguishable positions, or print the band instead ("5.0 ★ · 1 review"). Clamping the page parameter is even cheaper. Both are code changes and I'm not making them in a post. Full data if you want to check my arithmetic: the ranked shortlists that consume these numbers are at aiverse.mindutil.com/best — that's the one link I'll leave here, and yes, the page I just linked has its own defect sitting in its tag, which is a post for another day.
items.summary_html:
I have a directory of AI tools — 4,323 listings, live at aiverse.mindutil.com — and I keep publishing posts about how the numbers on my own pages are produced. Yesterday it was the click counter. Today I went looking for the bottom of my own list, and found that it doesn't have one.

The setup: two "browse everything" pages

My site has three pages whose job is to enumerate the catalog:

  • /ai-tools — the full directory, 24 cards per page, sorted by a mirrored read count
  • /top-ai-tools — "🏆 Top AI Tools", 48 cards per page, sorted by rating
  • /new-ai-tools — same grid, sorted by the publication date the upstream source gives me

All three render a numbered rank badge on each card on /top-ai-tools (1, 2, 3 …), and the header on that page carries a pill that says "Top 500".

So: how many pages is that, really?

/ai-tools       last page linked: 181  (180 × 24 + 3 = 4,323)
/top-ai-tools   last page linked:  91  (90 × 48 + 3 = 4,323)
/new-ai-tools   last page linked: 181

The arithmetic is fine. I checked it: I fetched all 91 pages of /top-ai-tools and all the rank badges came out as a contiguous run, 1 … 4,323, no duplicates, no gaps, 4,323 distinct listings, exactly the row count of the table. Pagination integrity: passes.

Then I asked for page 92.

Past the last page, the site stops telling the truth

GET /top-ai-tools?page=92 → HTTP 200. Not a 404, not a redirect to page 91. It renders the same header, the same "🏆 Top AI Tools" title, a rel="prev" link back to page 91, and zero cards.

GET /ai-tools?page=182 is worse, because that page still has a count in its intro copy:

</span>All AI Tools - Browse the Full Directory | AIVerse<span class="nt">
All AI Tools
"Explore 4,323 curated AI tools. Use the filters to narrow down by category, pricing and rating."
"4,323 tools found"
"No tools match your current search and filters. Try removing some filters or searching for something else."
 rel="canonical" href="https://aiverse.mindutil.com/ai-tools?page=182">
 name="robots" content="index, follow">

Same page, two contradictory sentences. The "4,323 tools found" line and the empty-state line come from different queries: the count is prisma.tool.count() over the filter (which ignores page), the grid is findMany() with skip/take. Off the end of the list, the count stays at 4,323 and the grid goes empty. The copy layer never hears about the other one.

And it's indexable, with a canonical that points at itself. Page 300: also 200. Page 999999: also 200, also index, follow. I tried six different out-of-range page numbers across four listings; every one answered 200 with robots: index, follow and a self-referencing canonical:

URL status cards robots canonical /ai-tools?page=182 200 0 index, follow ?page=182 /ai-tools?page=300 200 0 index, follow ?page=300 /ai-tools?page=9999 200 0 index, follow ?page=9999 /ai-tools?page=1e9 200 0 index, follow …?page=1000000000 /top-ai-tools?page=92 200 0 index, follow ?page=92 /free-ai-tools?page=200 200 0 index, follow ?page=200

?page=1e9 deserves its own line. The parser is:

export function parsePage(value: unknown): number {
  const n = Number(Array.isArray(value) ? value[0] : value);
  return Number.isFinite(n) && n >= 1 ? Math.floor(n) : 1;
}

Number("1e9") is finite and ≥ 1, so it becomes skip: 23999999976. 0, -1 and abc clamp to page 1 — those are handled; everything numeric just… keeps going. There's no upper bound because the handler doesn't know totalPages yet, and totalPages is computed inside the query it's supposed to guard.

Why I care: this is not only a UX thing. A parameter that accepts unbounded integers and answers 200 + index is a crawl-budget question — it's how a site with 4,443 sitemap URLs ends up with an effectively unlimited set of indexable URLs. The fix is four lines (clamp to totalPages, or return 404 past the end, and canonical any clamped page to the real one). I haven't deployed it, because today's rule for this series was "measure, don't touch the code".

The rank badge is a lie, but not in the way you'd expect

Back to /top-ai-tools. The badge next to each card is a real ordinal — it went 1 to 4,323 with no repeats. The problem is what it's an ordinal of. The order is:

case "rating":
  return [{ rating: "desc" }, { ratingCount: "desc" }];

Across the whole 4,323-row sweep there are only 258 distinct (rating, ratingCount) pairs. Which means most of my ranking is not a ranking.

rows whose (rating, ratingCount) pair is unique ........ 190  (4.4%)
rows that share their pair with at least one other row . 4,133  (95.6%)
biggest tie: (4.5, 2 reviews) = 695 rows, ranks 2,217–2,911
second:     (5.0, 1 review)  = 534 rows, ranks   222–755

695 listings are tied on both numbers at once, and I printed them as rank 2,217 through 2,911 in some order that is decided by the database's scan, not by anything I measured. Within a tie, SQLite gives whatever the scan gives — it's stable when the table doesn't change (I re-fetched page 50 twice, byte-identical), and undefined as a ranking.

That directly breaks the "Top 500" pill in the header. The boundary falls inside the (5.0, 1 review) block:

  • 279 rows with 5.0/1 review are inside the Top 500,
  • 255 rows with exactly the same two numbers are outside it,
  • and 497 of the first 500 rows share their numbers with another row.

The cut line between "top" and "not top" runs through a tie. Nobody decided it; the offset did.

The top of the list has its own problem. Rank 1 is Dall-E 2 with "Rated 6.3 out of 5" (3 reviews) — a rating that is arithmetically impossible on the scale the label claims, which comes from the same mirrored source as everything else, and which beats every 5.0 row precisely because rating: "desc" compares floats first. Rank 2 is Math99th at 5.0 with 28 reviews, tagged RIP AI — as are 83 of my first 500 rows. So the single highest-ranked tool on the site is an out-of-scale artifact, and the second is a product I've labeled as dead. At the other end, 129 rows have no rating at all and still got rank badges (4,195–4,323).

What I'm taking away
  1. A count and a list from the same filter are two different queries, and "N tools found" above an empty grid is a bug I can now reproduce on demand.
  2. index, follow + self-canonical on unbounded page numbers is a crawl surface I created by not clamping a number.
  3. An ordinal badge is only a claim of order if the sort key actually separates rows. With 258 distinct keys over 4,323 rows, 95.6% of my rank numbers describe a tie.
  4. If a page says "Top 500", the boundary must be a decision (a threshold, or a documented tie-break), not an artifact of skip.

The tie-break fix that costs nothing: append a stable unique key ({ id: "asc" }) so at least the order is reproducible rather than merely usually-stable — and then stop printing 4,323 rank numbers for 258 distinguishable positions, or print the band instead ("5.0 ★ · 1 review"). Clamping the page parameter is even cheaper. Both are code changes and I'm not making them in a post.

Full data if you want to check my arithmetic: the ranked shortlists that consume these numbers are at aiverse.mindutil.com/best — that's the one link I'll leave here, and yes, the page I just linked has its own defect sitting in its </code> tag, which is a post for another day.</p>
