items.title: From Biological Neurons to Liquid Foundation Models: Rethinking How We Build AI (Part 1)
items.summary: What happens when we look beyond conventional neural network architectures and take inspiration from biological systems? In this article we are exploring the research behind Liquid Neural Networks and the evolution of Liquid AI’s foundation models. 1. Introduction: Are Bigger Models Always Better? Over the past few years, the development of Artificial Intelligence has largely followed a familiar direction: bigger datasets, larger neural networks, more parameters, and increasingly powerful computing infrastructure. The success of Transformer-based architectures has reinforced this approach. Models have grown from millions to billions of parameters, while the computational resources required to train and serve them have increased considerably. But this raises an interesting engineering question: Do we always need larger models and more computational resources to build capable AI systems? Consider an environment where running a large language model on a cloud GPU is not an option. Perhaps the model needs to operate on a smartphone, an embedded processor, an industrial robot, or even inside a vehicle. In these environments, memory, processing power, latency, and energy consumption become important architectural constraints. This is where a different approach to building AI becomes interesting. One company exploring this direction is Liquid AI, whose research focuses on developing efficient foundation models using ideas from dynamical systems, signal processing, and numerical linear algebra. Interestingly, the company’s research has roots in something quite different from conventional AI development: the nervous system of a microscopic organism. To understand this connection, we first need to look at the research behind Liquid Neural Networks. 2. When Biology Inspires Artificial Intelligence Artificial Neural Networks were originally inspired by the way biological neurons communicate with one another. However, modern neural networks are mathematical and computational abstractions. They do not reproduce the complete complexity of biological brains. Researchers have continued exploring whether biological neural systems can offer alternative ways to design computational architectures. One particularly interesting example comes from Caenorhabditis elegans , commonly known as C. elegans. Anatomy of C. Elegans worm C. elegans is a microscopic nematode worm with a nervous system consisting of just 302 neurons in its adult hermaphrodite form. Neual Network mapping of C. Elegans Despite this relatively small nervous system, it can exhibit surprisingly complex behaviours, including navigation and responses to environmental stimuli. What makes this organism particularly interesting to neuroscience researchers is that its neural connections have been extensively mapped and studied. Researchers associated with MIT, including Ramin Hasani, Daniela Rus, and Alexander Amini, explored how the dynamics of such biological neural systems could inspire new artificial neural network architectures. The interesting observation was not simply that the organism had a small number of neurons. It was how those neurons behaved. Biological neurons do not necessarily operate as static computational units. Their activity evolves over time, influenced by incoming signals and the state of the surrounding neural system. This led researchers to investigate a different question: What if artificial neurons could have dynamics that evolve continuously over time rather than relying entirely on fixed computational behaviour? This research contributed to the development of Liquid Neural Networks. Reference: MIT News — “Liquid” machine-learning system adapts to changing conditions 3. Understanding Liquid Neural Networks (LNNs) Traditional neural networks generally learn their parameters during training. Once training is complete, those learned parameters are typically fixed during inference. For example, a conventional neural network processes an input through a series of mathematical transformations using learned weights and activation functions. Liquid Neural Networks explore a different approach. They use mathematical formulations in which the internal state of a neuron evolves continuously over time, with its dynamics influenced by incoming inputs. One of the foundational approaches in this research is the Liquid Time-Constant Network (LTC) . Unlike a conventional neural network that relies on fixed transformations, LTC networks use differential equations to describe how internal states change over time. At a conceptual level, we can represent this as: The equation The equation is a simplified conceptual representation of continuous-time neural dynamics, not the complete LTC formulation. The important distinction is that the network’s internal state is not treated as a static value. It evolves in response to incoming information. Why does this matter? Imagine an autonomous system processing information from its environment. The incoming information may change continuously. A camera might capture changing road conditions, a robot might encounter an unexpected obstacle, or a sensor might produce a fluctuating signal. A system that can model temporal dynamics may be better suited to processing such changing inputs. Liquid Neural Networks were designed to explore this kind of adaptability. Their potential advantages include: Temporal adaptability: Internal dynamics evolve in response to incoming signals. Compact representations: Expressive computational units can model complex temporal behaviour. Robustness: Their dynamics can offer useful properties when processing changing or noisy input streams. Interpretability: Their mathematical structure provides opportunities to analyze internal behaviour. It is important to understand that these properties do not automatically make every Liquid Neural Network more accurate or efficient than every conventional neural network. Performance depends on the task, architecture, training procedure, and deployment environment. Nevertheless, the research introduced an interesting alternative perspective: instead of relying exclusively on increasing network size, we can also investigate how individual computational units are designed. 4. What happens when we look beyond conventional neural network architectures and take inspiration from biological systems? In this article we are exploring the research behind Liquid Neural Networks and the evolution of Liquid AI’s foundation models.
1. Introduction: Are Bigger Models Always Better?

Over the past few years, the development of Artificial Intelligence has largely followed a familiar direction: bigger datasets, larger neural networks, more parameters, and increasingly powerful computing infrastructure.

The success of Transformer-based architectures has reinforced this approach. Models have grown from millions to billions of parameters, while the computational resources required to train and serve them have increased considerably.

But this raises an interesting engineering question:

Do we always need larger models and more computational resources to build capable AI systems?

Consider an environment where running a large language model on a cloud GPU is not an option. Perhaps the model needs to operate on a smartphone, an embedded processor, an industrial robot, or even inside a vehicle.

In these environments, memory, processing power, latency, and energy consumption become important architectural constraints.

This is where a different approach to building AI becomes interesting.

One company exploring this direction is Liquid AI, whose research focuses on developing efficient foundation models using ideas from dynamical systems, signal processing, and numerical linear algebra.

Interestingly, the company’s research has roots in something quite different from conventional AI development: the nervous system of a microscopic organism.

To understand this connection, we first need to look at the research behind Liquid Neural Networks.

2. When Biology Inspires Artificial Intelligence

Artificial Neural Networks were originally inspired by the way biological neurons communicate with one another.

However, modern neural networks are mathematical and computational abstractions. They do not reproduce the complete complexity of biological brains.

Researchers have continued exploring whether biological neural systems can offer alternative ways to design computational architectures.

One particularly interesting example comes from Caenorhabditis elegans, commonly known as C. elegans.

Anatomy of C. Elegans worm

C. elegans is a microscopic nematode worm with a nervous system consisting of just 302 neurons in its adult hermaphrodite form.

Neual Network mapping of C. Elegans

Despite this relatively small nervous system, it can exhibit surprisingly complex behaviours, including navigation and responses to environmental stimuli.

What makes this organism particularly interesting to neuroscience researchers is that its neural connections have been extensively mapped and studied.

Researchers associated with MIT, including Ramin Hasani, Daniela Rus, and Alexander Amini, explored how the dynamics of such biological neural systems could inspire new artificial neural network architectures.

The interesting observation was not simply that the organism had a small number of neurons.

It was how those neurons behaved.

Biological neurons do not necessarily operate as static computational units. Their activity evolves over time, influenced by incoming signals and the state of the surrounding neural system.

This led researchers to investigate a different question:

What if artificial neurons could have dynamics that evolve continuously over time rather than relying entirely on fixed computational behaviour?

This research contributed to the development of Liquid Neural Networks.

Reference: MIT News — “Liquid” machine-learning system adapts to changing conditions

3. Understanding Liquid Neural Networks (LNNs)

Traditional neural networks generally learn their parameters during training. Once training is complete, those learned parameters are typically fixed during inference.

For example, a conventional neural network processes an input through a series of mathematical transformations using learned weights and activation functions.

Liquid Neural Networks explore a different approach.

They use mathematical formulations in which the internal state of a neuron evolves continuously over time, with its dynamics influenced by incoming inputs.

One of the foundational approaches in this research is the Liquid Time-Constant Network (LTC).

Unlike a conventional neural network that relies on fixed transformations, LTC networks use differential equations to describe how internal states change over time.

At a conceptual level, we can represent this as:

The equation

The equation is a simplified conceptual representation of continuous-time neural dynamics, not the complete LTC formulation.

The important distinction is that the network’s internal state is not treated as a static value. It evolves in response to incoming information.

Why does this matter?

Imagine an autonomous system processing information from its environment.

The incoming information may change continuously. A camera might capture changing road conditions, a robot might encounter an unexpected obstacle, or a sensor might produce a fluctuating signal.

A system that can model temporal dynamics may be better suited to processing such changing inputs.

Liquid Neural Networks were designed to explore this kind of adaptability.

Their potential advantages include:

  • Temporal adaptability: Internal dynamics evolve in response to incoming signals.
  • Compact representations: Expressive computational units can model complex temporal behaviour.
  • Robustness: Their dynamics can offer useful properties when processing changing or noisy input streams.
  • Interpretability: Their mathematical structure provides opportunities to analyze internal behaviour.

It is important to understand that these properties do not automatically make every Liquid Neural Network more accurate or efficient than every conventional neural network. Performance depends on the task, architecture, training procedure, and deployment environment.

Nevertheless, the research introduced an interesting alternative perspective: instead of relying exclusively on increasing network size, we can also investigate how individual computational units are designed.

4. From Liquid Neural Networks to Liquid Foundation Models

Now comes the interesting transition.

Liquid Neural Networks and Liquid Foundation Models are related through the research direction, but they are not the same architecture.

Liquid AI was founded to explore new ways of building efficient and capable AI systems.

In September 2024, the company introduced its first generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs).

Rather than simply scaling conventional Transformer architectures, Liquid AI described its approach as building foundation models from first principles.

According to the company’s technical announcement, its LFMs use computational units rooted in three important areas:

  1. Dynamical systems
  2. Signal processing
  3. Numerical linear algebra

These fields provide mathematical tools for designing systems that process sequential information efficiently.

Why are these areas relevant?

Dynamical systems

Dynamical systems provide mathematical frameworks for describing how the state of a system changes over time.

This is particularly useful when modelling sequential information such as audio, video, sensor readings, and time-series data.

Signal processing

Signal processing focuses on analyzing and transforming signals.

Its mathematical foundations can be used to develop efficient operations for processing sequential data without necessarily relying on conventional attention-based architectures throughout the network.

Numerical linear algebra

This field deals with efficient mathematical operations involving vectors, matrices, and other numerical structures.

These operations form the computational foundation of many modern machine learning architectures.

The interesting part is how Liquid AI combines ideas from these fields to develop alternative computational building blocks for foundation models.

Its objective is not simply to make a smaller version of an existing LLM. It is to explore different architectural designs that can balance model capability, memory requirements, and inference efficiency.

Reference: Liquid AI — Introducing Liquid Foundation Models

5. What Makes Liquid Foundation Models Architecturally Interesting?

Let’s move one level deeper.

A common misconception is that Liquid Foundation Models are simply Liquid Neural Networks scaled up to billions of parameters.

That is not an accurate description.

Liquid AI’s foundation models represent a broader architectural direction that builds upon ideas developed through its earlier research.

A particularly interesting example is LFM2, introduced in July 2025.

LFM2 uses a hybrid architecture combining two types of computational blocks:

  • Gated short-range convolution blocks.
  • Grouped Query Attention (GQA) blocks.

The published LFM2 architecture contains 16 blocks:

  • 10 double-gated short convolution blocks.
  • 6 grouped-query attention blocks.

Why combine these approaches?

1) Gated short convolutions

Convolutions are commonly associated with computer vision, but they can also be used to process sequential information.

In LFM2, gated short convolutions provide an efficient mechanism for processing local patterns in a sequence.

The gating operations allow the computation to be modulated by the input.

In simplified terms, the model can use input-dependent gates to control how information flows through these computational blocks.

2) Grouped Query Attention

Attention mechanisms allow models to identify relationships between different positions in a sequence.

Grouped Query Attention is an attention variant that shares key-value representations across groups of query heads.

This reduces the memory and computational requirements associated with maintaining separate key-value representations for every attention head.

Why combine them?

The hybrid architecture uses different computational mechanisms for different purposes.

Short convolutions provide efficient local sequence processing, while attention blocks help model relationships across a broader context.

This is an important architectural decision because designing models for edge deployment requires balancing several competing requirements:

  1. Model quality.

2. Inference latency.

3. Memory consumption.

4. Hardware compatibility.

5. Computational efficiency.

Liquid AI’s LFM2 technical report describes how hardware-in-the-loop architecture search was used to identify architectures under edge latency and memory constraints.

In other words, the architecture is not designed independently of its deployment environment. The target hardware and its computational characteristics influence the design process itself.

This is a particularly interesting direction for developers working on efficient AI inference.

References: LFM2 — Official technical report | Liquid AI — Introducing LFM2

6. The Bigger Picture: Intelligence Beyond the Cloud

There is an important idea connecting all these developments.

For years, much of the progress in generative AI has been associated with increasingly powerful centralized computing infrastructure.

But not every AI application can depend on a remote server.

Consider devices such as:

  • Smartphones.
  • Industrial robots.
  • Autonomous systems.
  • Smart appliances.
  • Automotive infotainment systems.

These devices operate under different computational constraints.

They may have limited memory, restricted power budgets, varying connectivity, and strict latency requirements.

Running capable AI models directly on these devices requires more than simply reducing parameter counts.

It requires careful consideration of the entire inference pipeline, including model architecture, hardware acceleration, memory management, and runtime optimization.

This is where efficient foundation models become particularly relevant.

Liquid AI’s work represents one attempt to explore this direction: designing foundation models with the computational characteristics of their target deployment environments in mind.

And this brings us to an interesting real-world application.

What happens when these ideas move beyond research papers and model benchmarks and become part of an actual production vehicle?

That is where Mercedes-Benz enters the picture.

Mercedes-Benz & Liquid AI

We’ll explore that in Part 2.

Further Reading

If you want to explore the research behind this article, these are good starting points:

  1. MIT — Liquid Machine Learning Systems
  2. Liquid AI — From Liquid Neural Networks to Liquid Foundation Models
  3. Liquid AI — First Generation of Liquid Foundation Models
  4. Liquid AI — LFM2 Architecture and Technical Report
This article is intended as a technical exploration of the research and architectural ideas behind Liquid AI. The biological inspiration discussed here should not be interpreted as evidence that every Liquid Foundation Model directly reproduces biological neuron firing patterns.
